synonyms: ["Ibd", "Inflammatory bowel disease (acute flares)", "Inflammatory bowel disease (flare-ups)", "Inflammatory bowel flare-ups", "Chronic Inflammatory Bowel Disease", "Chronic IBD", "Inflammatory Bowel Syndrome", "Long-term Bowel Inflammation"]
conventional_description: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) is a term that mainly covers Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis - both are chronic conditions where the immune system mistakenly attacks the digestive tract, causing inflammation, ulcers, and tissue damage. Typical symptoms include persistent diarrhea often mixed with blood or mucus, cramping abdominal pain, urgent bowel movements, fatigue, and weight loss. Diagnosis usually involves a colonoscopy with biopsies, imaging studies, and stool tests to rule out infection.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment aims to reduce inflammation and prevent flares. Mild to moderate cases often start with aminosalicylates. Corticosteroids are used for short-term flare control but aren't suitable long-term. Immunomodulators and biologic drugs (like anti-TNF agents) target the immune system to maintain remission. In severe cases or when complications arise, surgery may be needed to remove damaged portions of the intestine.
tcm_understanding:
TCM sees IBD primarily as a disorder of the Spleen and Stomach's ability to transform food and fluids. When these organs are weak, they fail to separate clear from turbid, allowing dampness to accumulate and sink into the Large Intestine. This dampness is the root of the sticky, mucousy stools and the heavy, dragging sensation so many patients describe.
What happens next depends on the individual. If the body is overheated - from diet, stress, or infection - dampness combines with heat to create a fiery, urgent pattern: bloody stools, burning anus, constant urge to go. This is the Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner pattern, and it demands cooling, drying herbs like Bai Tou Weng and Huang Lian to clear the intestinal fire.
If the constitution is cold and exhausted, however, dampness turns into a sluggish, chronic picture. The Spleen becomes too weak to hold things in, leading to chronic loose stools and bloating, while the Kidney's warming fire dims, causing early-morning diarrhea and cold limbs. Here, the treatment strategy flips entirely - warming, strengthening formulas like Si Shen Wan are needed, not cold bitter herbs.
Emotional stress adds another layer. The Liver governs the smooth flow of Qi, and when frustration or anxiety causes it to stagnate, it can invade the already weak Spleen, trapping dampness in the gut. This stress-triggered pattern often needs calming, moving formulas like Xiao Yao San to untie the knot. In long-standing cases, chronic inflammation can even lead to fixed, stabbing pain from blood stasis, requiring herbs that move blood and stop pain.

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first listens carefully to the story of the bowel movements-their urgency, appearance, and what makes them better or worse. The presence or absence of heat signs, such as burning, bright blood, or fever, immediately helps separate hot patterns from cold or deficient ones. That initial distinction narrows the field sharply before even looking at the tongue or pulse.
When the stool is bloody, purulent, and accompanied by a burning sensation in the anus and a constant urge to go (tenesmus), the picture points to Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner. The tongue is red with a thick yellow greasy coating, and the pulse feels slippery and rapid. This pattern is acute and fiery, demanding clearing and cooling strategies.
If instead the main complaint is chronic loose stools, bloating after eating, and a heavy tiredness that never lifts, Spleen Deficiency with Dampness is the likely driver. The tongue is pale and puffy with a white coat, and the pulse is weak and soft. Here there is no burning or heat-just a sluggish digestive system that cannot transform fluids properly, leaving dampness to pool in the gut.
When symptoms flare predictably with emotional stress-frustration, worry, or anger-and the person notices abdominal distension that moves around, the pattern shifts to Obstruction of the Spleen by Dampness with Liver Qi Stagnation. The tongue may be slightly red on the sides, and the pulse feels wiry. The practitioner will ask about mood and tension because the Liver’s smooth flow is clearly involved.
Long-standing IBD can lead to Qi and Blood Stagnation, where pain becomes fixed and stabbing rather than shifting, and the stool may contain dark, clotted blood. The tongue shows purple spots or a dusky body, and the pulse is choppy.
Finally, if the illness has worn down the body’s deep reserves, Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency emerges with cold limbs, a sore lower back, and the hallmark early-morning diarrhea that sends the person rushing to the bathroom at dawn.

patterns.symptoms: ["Stools with blood, mucus, or pus", "Burning pain in the anus during and after bowel movements", "Constant urge to defecate with little relief (tenesmus)", "Abdominal cramping, worse with pressure", "Dark, scanty urine", "Thirst with no desire to drink much"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried foods, Spicy foods and alcohol, Hot, humid weather, Stress and frustration, Raw and cold foods
patterns.better_with: Light, bland meals (congee), Warm water, not iced, Gentle walking, Rest and avoiding overexertion
patterns.why_this_happens: Dampness and Heat are two pathogens that easily combine and sink to the Lower Burner, where they get trapped in the Large Intestine. The Heat irritates the intestinal lining, causing bleeding and a burning sensation, while the Dampness makes the stools sticky, foul, and full of mucus. Together they block the normal downward flow of Qi, creating the intense cramping and the constant, frustrating urge to go (tenesmus) that feels like you can never fully empty your bowels.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a yellow greasy coating, thickest at the root. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and rapid (数 shuò), often soggy (濡 rú), more pronounced at the rear (Chi) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Damp-Heat is a combination of excess moisture and heat that gets trapped in the Lower Burner. Greasy, spicy, and damp-producing foods (like dairy and sugar) directly add to this pathogenic mix, while hot, humid weather makes it harder for the body to clear dampness. Stress stagnates Liver Qi, which can further obstruct the intestines. Light, bland meals and rest reduce the burden on the Spleen and Intestines, allowing the body to gradually resolve the dampness and heat. Gentle movement helps Qi circulate without creating more heat. Warm water supports digestion without adding cold that would congeal dampness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and raw foods that create more dampness and heat. Focus on lightly cooked, easy-to-digest meals like rice porridge (congee) with a little ginger. Drink warm water instead of iced beverages, and avoid dairy and sugar. Gentle walking helps Qi flow without taxing the body. Keep the abdomen warm and avoid prolonged sitting in damp environments.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is weak, it struggles to transform food and fluids into usable Qi and Blood. This leaves unprocessed moisture to accumulate as internal Dampness, which then sinks into the intestines. The result is chronic loose stools, bloating, and a heavy, tired feeling - a cycle where the lingering Dampness further bogs down an already tired Spleen.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, white greasy coating, moist surface. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and slow (Huan), soft and lacking force.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: A weak Spleen cannot cope with cold or raw foods, which directly injure its warming, transformative function. Dairy, greasy, and sweet foods are inherently dampening and add to the internal Dampness already bogging the system down. Overeating simply overwhelms a tired Spleen, while damp weather mirrors the internal environment and worsens symptoms. On the other hand, warm, cooked meals provide easily digestible nourishment that supports Spleen Yang, small meals lighten the workload, and gentle movement - unlike a sedentary lifestyle - activates Qi to help dry out Dampness. Ginger and similar warming spices directly warm the middle burner to aid digestion.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Make warm, cooked foods the foundation of your diet - think congee, stews, and soups. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods, as well as dairy and excess sweets, which all generate Dampness. Eat small, regular meals to avoid overwhelming a tired Spleen, and incorporate gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi to keep Qi flowing and Dampness at bay.

patterns.why_this_happens: In long-standing IBD, the Spleen's ability to transform food and fluids becomes exhausted, leading to chronic loose stools and fatigue. patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat only warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees. Avoid all raw, cold, and iced items. Keep the abdomen and lower back warm with a belly band or hot water bottle. Gentle daily walking helps move Qi without exhausting Yang. Moxibustion at home on the lower abdomen can be very supportive.

faqs.question: How does TCM treat IBD differently from Western medicine?
faqs.answer: Instead of a single anti-inflammatory approach, TCM identifies the exact pattern of imbalance causing your symptoms - whether it's damp-heat, cold deficiency, or stagnation - and tailors herbs and acupuncture to correct that specific root. This means two people with IBD might receive completely different treatments based on their tongue, pulse, and symptom details.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help with IBD pain and urgency?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture can calm intestinal spasms, reduce pain, and regulate bowel movements by working on points like Tianshu ST-25 and Zusanli ST-36. Many patients feel a soothing effect during the session itself. It's especially helpful for stress-triggered flares and can be used safely alongside your regular medications.

faqs.question: What Chinese herbs are used for IBD?
faqs.answer: The herbs depend entirely on your pattern. For hot, bloody flares, bitter-cold herbs like Bai Tou Weng and Huang Lian clear damp-heat. For chronic, loose stools with fatigue, warming tonics like Bai Zhu and Bu Gu Zhi strengthen the Spleen and Kidney. A licensed practitioner will adjust your formula as your symptoms change - never self-prescribe, especially with active inflammation.

faqs.question: Will I have to change my diet with TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: Diet is a cornerstone of TCM care for IBD. Across all patterns, you'll be advised to eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods and avoid raw, cold, greasy, and spicy items that burden the Spleen. Specific recommendations - like adding ginger or avoiding dairy - will be tailored to your pattern. Small, frequent meals are almost always encouraged.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results with TCM?
faqs.answer: Many people notice less urgency, pain, and fewer bowel movements within the first 2-4 weeks of herbs and acupuncture. Stopping the cycle of flares and rebuilding digestive strength takes longer - typically 3-6 months of consistent treatment. The goal is not just symptom relief but a lasting reduction in flare frequency and severity.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside my biologic or immunosuppressant medication?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM is often used alongside conventional IBD medications. However, it's essential that both your gastroenterologist and TCM practitioner know the full list of everything you're taking. Some herbs have mild immune-modulating effects, so your team should monitor your response. Never stop or adjust prescribed medications without medical supervision.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe during an active IBD flare?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture and herbal formulas can be very effective during a flare to calm inflammation and stop bleeding, but they must be prescribed by a qualified practitioner who can distinguish between hot and cold patterns. If you have severe pain, high fever, or heavy bleeding, seek urgent medical care first - TCM can then support recovery once the acute emergency is ruled out.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicines in the treatment of ulcerative colitis: a review
research.description: This narrative review summarizes the pharmacological mechanisms and clinical evidence for Chinese herbal formulas, including Bai Tou Weng Tang and Shen Ling Bai Zhu San, in ulcerative colitis. It highlights anti-inflammatory, mucosal-protective, and immune-modulating effects, while noting the need for more rigorous RCTs.
research.periodical: Zhang, Y., et al. Chinese herbal medicines in the treatment of ulcerative colitis: a review. Frontiers in Pharmacology, 2022.

research.title: Acupuncture for ulcerative colitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: A meta-analysis of 13 RCTs involving over 1,000 patients found that acupuncture as an adjunct to conventional therapy significantly improved clinical remission rates and reduced disease activity scores compared to sham acupuncture or medication alone. The quality of evidence was moderate due to risk of bias.
research.periodical: Ji, J., et al. Acupuncture for ulcerative colitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine, 2019.

research.title: Efficacy of Bai Tou Weng Tang combined with mesalazine in treating active ulcerative colitis: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: In a 12-week RCT of 120 patients with mild-to-moderate active ulcerative colitis, the combination of Bai Tou Weng Tang and mesalazine achieved a significantly higher clinical response rate (78.3%) than mesalazine alone (56.7%), with fewer adverse events. The herbal formula was well tolerated.
research.periodical: Wang, L., et al. Efficacy of Bai Tou Weng Tang combined with mesalazine in treating active ulcerative colitis: a randomized controlled trial. Chinese Journal of Integrated Traditional and Western Medicine, 2020.
